title: Spicy Food May Mute Intense Pain
paragraphs: For many people, eating spicy food is a painful experience. However, a new study from China suggests that the burning sensation caused by chili peppers may actually help reduce the feeling of intense pain elsewhere in the body.

The study was carried out by a team of researchers including Zhou Yang of Chongqing Normal University, and it was published in the journal Physiology & Behavior in 2026. It involved 48 healthy young adults who were recruited from a university campus. People with chronic pain, mental health conditions or digestive problems such as stomach ulcers were not included.

Each participant visited the laboratory twice, about a week apart. First, the researchers adjusted an infrared laser for each person so that it produced either a mild heat pain or an intense heat pain on the back of the hand. On one visit, the participants held a piece of gelatin containing chili powder in their mouths for five minutes, without chewing or swallowing it. On the other visit, they held a piece of plain gelatin. They then received 40 laser pulses on their hand and rated how intense and unpleasant each one felt.

The researchers found that after holding the chili gelatin, the participants rated the intense laser pulses as less painful and less unpleasant than after holding the plain gelatin. However, the chili made no difference to how they felt the mild pulses.

The participants also answered questions about their diets. People who preferred spicier food tended to be less sensitive to pain, feared pain less and said they could tolerate more pain. However, this was only a correlation, which could be explained by other factors such as genetics or culture.

The researchers suggested several possible explanations for the results. The burning in the mouth may have triggered a natural process in which one painful feeling reduces another, known as conditioned pain modulation. Capsaicin, the substance that makes chili peppers hot, may also encourage the release of endorphins, the body's natural painkillers. Alternatively, the burning sensation may simply have distracted the participants. Because the study did not measure attention, the researchers could not rule this out.
The study was small, and all the participants were young, healthy students in China. As a result, the findings may not apply to older adults or people with chronic pain.
